claim: Complexin cross-links multiple pre-fusion SNARE complexes via a trans interaction to function as a clamp on SNARE-mediated neurotransmitter release.
source: We have previously proposed that complexin cross-links multiple pre-fusion SNARE complexes via a trans interaction to function as a clamp on SNARE-mediated neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is the authors' previously proposed model that they are defending in this manuscript.

claim: A recent NMR study was unable to detect the trans clamping interaction of complexin.
source: A recent NMR study was unable to detect the trans clamping interaction of complexin and therefore questioned the previous interpretation of the fluorescence resonance energy transfer and isothermal titration calorimetry data on which the trans clamping model was originally based.
evidence: Reference to findings from Trimbuch et al. (2014) study.

claim: The fusion of a synaptic vesicle to release neurotransmitters is mediated by the SNARE complex.
source: The fusion of a synaptic vesicle to release the neurotransmitters is mediated by the SNARE (Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment protein REceptor) complex, which forms between vesicle and target membranes as v-SNAREs emanating from transport vesicles assemble with t-SNAREs emanating from target membranes (Sollner et al., 1993; Weber et al., 1998; Jahn and Scheller, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Synaptotagmin and complexin are key proteins regulating SNARE-mediated fusion at the synapse.
source: Key proteins regulating SNARE-mediated fusion at the synapse are the calcium sensor synaptotagmin and complexin (CPX) (Brose et al., 1992; McMahon et al., 1995; Fernandez-Chacon et al., 2001; Giraudo et al., 2006; Sudhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Complexin inhibits the spontaneous release of neurotransmitters.
source: Genetic and physiological studies in a number of model systems show that CPX inhibits the spontaneous release of neurotransmitters and is also essential for synchronous exocytosis (Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Maximov et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genetic and physiological studies.

claim: Complexin is essential for synchronous exocytosis.
source: Genetic and physiological studies in a number of model systems show that CPX inhibits the spontaneous release of neurotransmitters and is also essential for synchronous exocytosis (Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Maximov et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genetic and physiological studies.

claim: Complexin 'clamps' the SNARE assembly process to prevent the continuous release of neurotransmitters.
source: CPX 'clamps' the SNARE assembly process to prevent the continuous release of neurotransmitters (Giraudo et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giraudo et al. (2006).

claim: Complexin stabilizes the SNAREs in an 'intermediate' energetic state in which the four helix bundle is about 50% zippered.
source: It does so by stabilizing the SNAREs in an otherwise unavailable 'intermediate' energetic state in which the four helix bundle is about 50% zippered (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al. (2011).

claim: The CPX central helix binds one SNAREpin while the accessory helix extends away and bridges to a second SNAREpin.
source: We found that the CPX central helix (CPXcen, the SNARE-binding domain) binds one SNAREpin while the accessory helix (CPXacc, the clamping domain) extends away and bridges to a second SNAREpin.
evidence: Based on X-ray crystal structure analysis reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: The CPXacc interacts with the t-SNARE in the second SNAREpin, occupying the v-SNARE binding site, thus inhibiting the full assembly of the SNARE complex.
source: The CPXacc interacts with the t-SNARE in the second SNAREpin, occupying the v-SNARE binding site, thus inhibiting the full assembly of the SNARE complex.
evidence: Based on structural and biochemical analysis from previous work.

claim: The intermolecular trans clamping interaction of CPX organizes the SNAREpins into a 'zig-zag' topology that is incompatible with opening a fusion pore.
source: Further, the intermolecular trans clamping interaction of CPX organizes the SNAREpins into a 'zig-zag' topology that is incompatible with opening a fusion pore (Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: CPX-48 binds to the post-fusion SNARE complex with a Kd of 43 ± 7 nM.
source: under our experimental conditions, the Kd for CPX-48 binding to the post-fusion SNARE complex was 43 ± 7 nM (Figure 1A, Table 1)
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments in this study, shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: CPX-48 binds to the pre-fusion SNAREΔ60 with a Kd of 457 ± 47 nM.
source: We found further that CPX-48 bound the pre-fusion SNAREΔ60 with a Kd = 457 ± 47 nM (Figure 1B, Table 1)
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments in this study, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: CPX-48 binds to the pre-fusion SNAREΔ60 about five times more tightly than reported by Trimbuch et al. (2014).
source: We found further that CPX-48 bound the pre-fusion SNAREΔ60 with a Kd = 457 ± 47 nM (Figure 1B, Table 1), or about five times more tightly than reported by Trimbuch et al. (2014).
evidence: Comparison of current ITC data with previously published values.

claim: A 1.5 molar excess of CPX-48 ensures near saturation (~96%) of the central helix binding site.
source: These binding constants ensure the near saturation (∼96%) of the central helix binding site under the conditions (1.5 molar excess of CPX-48) reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).
evidence: Calculated from the measured binding constants.

claim: Hydrophobic mutations (D27L, E34F, R37A) in CPXacc increase the binding affinity approximately eightfold stronger than wild-type.
source: Hydrophobic mutations (D27L, E34F, R37A) increased the binding affinity (approximately eightfold stronger than the wild-type, Table 1)
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments reported in Kümmel et al. (2011), referenced in Table 1.

claim: Introduction of charged residues (A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) in CPXacc abolishes the interaction with t-SNARE.
source: while the introduction of charged residues (A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) abolished the interaction (Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: Full-length CPX binds to blocked SNAREΔ60 with a binding affinity of 15.2 ± 1.4 µM.
source: We found that CPX binds to the blocked SNAREΔ60 with a binding affinity of 15.2 ± 1.4 µM (Figure 2A, Table 1)
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments in this study using 2.5-3-fold molar excess of CPX-48, shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: CPX26-83 binds to blocked SNAREΔ60 with a Kd of 23.9 ± 0.1 µM.
source: We have now additionally carried out the ITC experiments with the minimal functional domain (CPX26–83) and find that this truncated version also binds to the blocked SNAREΔ60, albeit with slightly weaker affinity (Kd = 23.9 ± 0.1 µM) compared with full-length CPX (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments in this study, shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Titration of scCPX into unblocked SNAREΔ60 results in a thermal graph characteristic of a reaction involving multiple binding sites.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, titration of scCPX into the unblocked SNAREΔ60 results in a thermal graph characteristic of a reaction involving multiple binding sites, demonstrating that CPX has more than one binding site per SNAREΔ60 complex.
evidence: Observed in ITC experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CPX has more than one binding site per SNAREΔ60 complex.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, titration of scCPX into the unblocked SNAREΔ60 results in a thermal graph characteristic of a reaction involving multiple binding sites, demonstrating that CPX has more than one binding site per SNAREΔ60 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the ITC data showing multiple binding sites in Figure 3A.

claim: The ITC data for scCPX binding to SNAREΔ60 can be best approximated using independent thermodynamic parameters for CPXcen and CPXacc interaction, assuming both SNAREΔ60 and scCPX are bivalent.
source: The data can be best approximated using the independent thermodynamic parameters for the CPXcen and CPXacc interaction, with the assumption that both the truncated SNAREΔ60 and scCPX are bivalent (Figure 3B).
evidence: Analysis of ITC data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The low FRET state observed in the pre-fusion SNAREpin corresponds to the 'angled' conformation of CPXacc.
source: The FRET data were consistent with the CPXacc locating parallel to the SNARE complex in the fully-assembled SNARE complex, but moving away from the SNAREs in the pre-fusion half-zippered complex (Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on FRET analysis reported in previous work.

claim: A well-defined 'high' and 'low' FRET state is observed for CPX bound to the post- and pre-fusion SNARE using two different FRET pairs with different R0 values.
source: We observe a well-defined 'high' and 'low' FRET state for CPX bound to the post- and pre-fusion SNARE using two different FRET pairs with different R0 values (Stilbene/Bimane, R0 ∼27Å and Bimane/Oregon Green, R0 ∼38Å)
evidence: Based on FRET experiments reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: The FRET distances in CPX-SNARE complexes match very well with the predicted distance in the pre- and post-fusion crystal structures.
source: and the FRET distances in these CPX–SNARE complexes match very well with the predicted distance in the pre- and post-fusion crystal structures (Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison of FRET-derived distances with crystal structure predictions.

claim: A completely unstructured CPX would result in a higher FRET signal than a more structured form.
source: Further, a study by Choi et al. suggests that a completely unstructured CPX would result in a higher FRET signal than a more structured form (Choi et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al. (2011).

claim: The decrease in FRET efficiency for CPX bound to SNAREΔ60 is not consistent with increased disorder.
source: so the decrease in FRET efficiency for CPX bound to SNAREΔ60 is not consistent with increased disorder.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with expected behavior of unstructured proteins.

claim: Acceptor placed at residue 31 on CPXacc shows weaker FRET compared with residue 38.
source: For both the FRET pairs tested, acceptor placed at residue 31 on CPXacc shows weaker FRET compared with residue 38, consistent with the idea that the CPXacc extends away from the pre-fusion SNARE complex, with dye on residue 31 locating further away from the donor (on SNAP25) than the dye on residue 38 (Kümmel et al., 2011, Figure 4).
evidence: Based on FRET experiments reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: The same well-defined low FRET state (~15% FRET) is observed for CPX bound to SNAREΔ69, SNAREΔ65, or SNAREΔ60 complexes.
source: In the accompanying paper (Krishnakumar et al., 2011), we tested the effect of VAMP truncation on the orientation of CPXacc and observed the same well-defined low FRET state (∼15% FRET) for CPX bound to SNARE∆69, SNARE∆65, or SNARE∆60 complexes (Krishnakumar et al., 2011, Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on FRET experiments reported in Krishnakumar et al. (2011).

claim: The FRET signal observed in the 'low' FRET state is higher than the FRET signal obtained when using CPX-GPGP with enhanced flexibility.
source: Finally, the FRET signal we observed in the 'low' FRET state is higher than the FRET signal obtained when we used a CPX construct with enhanced flexibility (CPX–GPGP) in which a helix-breaking GPGP linker was inserted between the central and accessory helices of CPX for either SNARE∆60 or the post-fusion SNARE complex (Kümmel et al., 2011, Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on FRET experiments with CPX-GPGP mutant reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: The GPGP insertion in CPX results in a dramatic decrease in the FRET signal, with the CPXacc locating further away from both SNAREΔ60 and the SNARE complex.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the GPGP insertion results in a dramatic decrease in the FRET signal, with the CPXacc locating further away from both SNARE∆60 and the SNARE complex.
evidence: Based on FRET experiments with Bimane/Oregon green FRET pair shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased flexibility does not explain the decreased FRET signal in the pre-fusion truncated SNARE complex.
source: These data suggest that the increased flexibility does not explain the decreased FRET signal in the pre-fusion truncated SNARE complex.
evidence: Inference from FRET data comparing wild-type and CPX-GPGP mutant.

claim: CPX26-48 alone does not interact with SNAREΔ60 as measured by ITC.
source: Using NMR, Trimbuch et al. were unable to detect any interaction between a peptide corresponding to CPXacc only (CPX26–48) and SNARE∆60 (Trimbuch et al., 2014). This experiment is in agreement with our ITC measurements, which did not detect an interaction between SNARE∆60 and CPX26–48 alone (unpublished).
evidence: Based on unpublished ITC measurements by the authors.

claim: CPXacc (residues 26-48) by itself is unfolded.
source: For example, our circular dichroism (CD) measurements showed that CPXacc (residues 26–48) by itself is unfolded, but CPX26–83 forms a stable α-helical structure (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on CD measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CPX26-83 forms a stable α-helical structure.
source: For example, our circular dichroism (CD) measurements showed that CPXacc (residues 26–48) by itself is unfolded, but CPX26–83 forms a stable α-helical structure (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on CD measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CPX26-83/SNAREΔ60 complexes begin to oligomerize at concentrations of 25-50 μM.
source: Dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis (Figure 5B, black circles) similarly suggests that CPX26–83/SNAREΔ60 complexes begin to oligomerize at the concentration regime used in Trimbuch et al. (25–50 μM).
evidence: Based on DLS analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The DLS data are consistent with a model predicting the size of oligomers which incorporates the Kd of ~25 µM obtained from ITC analysis of CPX26-83 and blocked SNAREΔ60 interaction.
source: The DLS data are consistent with a model predicting the size of the oligomers (see 'Materials and methods' for details on the model, Figure 5B, black line) which incorporates the Kd of ∼25 µM obtained from our ITC analysis of the CPX26–83 and blocked SNAREΔ60 interaction.
evidence: Comparison of DLS data with theoretical model based on ITC-derived Kd values.

claim: Introducing non-clamping mutations (ncCPX26-83; A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) in CPXacc results in only a small change in the apparent size of CPX-SNARE complexes.
source: In contrast, we observe only a small change in the apparent size if we disrupt the binding of CPXacc to t-SNARE either by introducing non-clamping mutations (ncCPX26–83; A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) in CPXacc (Figure 5B, blue circles)
evidence: Based on DLS analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blocking the t-SNARE groove using a fully assembled ternary SNARE complex results in only a small change in the apparent size of CPX-SNARE complexes.
source: In contrast, we observe only a small change in the apparent size if we disrupt the binding of CPXacc to t-SNARE either by introducing non-clamping mutations (ncCPX26–83; A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) in CPXacc (Figure 5B, blue circles) or by blocking the t-SNARE groove using a fully assembled ternary SNARE complex (Figure 5B, green circles).
evidence: Based on DLS analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The inhibitory function of CPX has not been observed in the autaptic system.
source: Specifically, the inhibitory function of CPX has not been observed in the autaptic system: that is, both evoked and spontaneous release are reduced in CPX TKO mice (Reim et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2008; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in CPX TKO mice.

claim: Rodent mass cultured neurons with reduced CPX expression and invertebrates lacking CPX exhibit reduced evoked release and enhanced spontaneous release.
source: In contrast, other preparations like rodent mass cultured neurons with reduced CPX expression and invertebrates lacking CPX exhibit reduced evoked release and enhanced spontaneous release (Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Yang et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in different model systems.

claim: CPX mutants that enhanced the CPXacc-SNARE interactions (super-clamp) resulted in reductions in spontaneous release compared with wild-type CPX controls in rescue experiments with rodent mass cultured neurons.
source: In rescue experiments with rodent mass cultured neurons in which CPX was knocked down, CPX mutants that either enhanced or disrupted the CPXacc–SNARE interactions (super-clamp and poor clamp, respectively) resulted in corresponding reductions and enhancements in spontaneous release compared with wild-type CPX controls (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al. (2010) rescue experiments.

claim: CPX mutants that disrupted the CPXacc-SNARE interactions (poor clamp) resulted in enhancements in spontaneous release compared with wild-type CPX controls in rescue experiments with rodent mass cultured neurons.
source: In rescue experiments with rodent mass cultured neurons in which CPX was knocked down, CPX mutants that either enhanced or disrupted the CPXacc–SNARE interactions (super-clamp and poor clamp, respectively) resulted in corresponding reductions and enhancements in spontaneous release compared with wild-type CPX controls (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al. (2010) rescue experiments.

claim: CPX-GPGP mutants disrupt the ability of CPX to clamp spontaneous release at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Using genetic rescue approaches, CPX mutants predicted to prevent the formation of the zig-zag array (CPX–GPGP) disrupt the ability of CPX to clamp spontaneous release, while mutations predicted to enhance the CPXacc–t-SNARE interaction (super-clamp mutation) exhibit a strong clamping ability (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho et al. (2014) genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Super-clamp mutations predicted to enhance the CPXacc-t-SNARE interaction exhibit a strong clamping ability at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Using genetic rescue approaches, CPX mutants predicted to prevent the formation of the zig-zag array (CPX–GPGP) disrupt the ability of CPX to clamp spontaneous release, while mutations predicted to enhance the CPXacc–t-SNARE interaction (super-clamp mutation) exhibit a strong clamping ability (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho et al. (2014) genetic rescue experiments.

claim: The inhibitory and activating functions of CPX may be separable.
source: These results taken together are consistent with a CPX cross-linking model mediating the CPX clamping function to regulate spontaneous release, even though recent reports suggest that the inhibitory and activating functions of CPX may be separable (Yang et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent reports.

claim: Introducing two (L41E, A44E) or four (A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) negatively charged mutations in the mammalian CPXacc abolishes or severely diminishes the interaction of CPXacc with the mammalian or Drosophila t-SNARE.
source: Introducing two (L41E, A44E) or four (A30E, A31E, L41E, A44E) negatively charged mutations in the mammalian CPXacc has been shown to entirely abolish or severely diminish the interaction of CPXacc with the mammalian or Drosophila t-SNARE, respectively (Kümmel et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kümmel et al. (2011) and Cho et al. (2014).

claim: Mutations that abolish CPXacc-t-SNARE interaction abrogate the clamping function of CPX in both in vitro cell-cell fusion assay and in vivo rescue experiments with knockdown neurons.
source: Consistent with this finding, the similar mutations have been shown to abrogate the clamping function of CPX in both in vitro cell–cell fusion assay (Kümmel et al., 2011) and in vivo rescue experiments with knockdown neurons (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kümmel et al. (2011) and Yang et al. (2010).

claim: Increasing the hydrophobicity of CPXacc enhances the clamping function of CPX.
source: Further, in contrast to the electrostatic model, increasing the hydrophobicity of CPXacc has been shown to enhance the clamping function of CPX (Yang et al., 2010; Kümmel et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ITC binding experiments with blocked SNARE complexes have corroborated the interaction of CPXacc with the t-SNARE groove in a pre-fusion SNARE complex.
source: Specifically, ITC binding experiments with blocked SNARE complexes, where a 2.5–3-fold excess of blocking peptide was present, have corroborated the interaction of CPXacc with the t-SNARE groove in a pre-fusion (truncated) SNARE complex as observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2 and Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on ITC experiments shown in Figure 2 and comparison with crystal structure.

claim: Titration of scCPX into unblocked truncated SNARE complex revealed multiple binding sites consistent with independent binding sites for CPXcen and scCPXacc.
source: Additionally, titration of scCPX into unblocked truncated SNARE complex revealed multiple binding sites consistent with independent binding sites for CPXcen and scCPXacc, thus describing the essential feature of the trans clamping interaction of CPX (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on ITC experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: FRET analysis with flexible CPX construct (CPX-GPGP) has demonstrated that the low FRET state corresponding to the angled conformation is due to discrete conformational change and not because of increased CPX flexibility.
source: FRET analysis (using two FRET pairs with different R0 values) with 'flexible' CPX construct (CPX–GPGP) has clearly demonstrated that the low FRET state corresponding to the angled conformation, which describes the trans clamping interaction, is due to discrete conformational change and not because of increased CPX flexibility (Figure 4 and Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on FRET experiments shown in Figure 4 and Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: Mutations in CPX that are predicted to prevent the formation of the SNAREpin array disrupt the ability of CPX to clamp spontaneous release in Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Lastly, the physiological relevance of the insertion model was established by independent genetic rescue experiments in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, wherein mutations in CPX that are predicted to prevent the formation of the SNAREpin array were found to disrupt the ability of CPX to clamp spontaneous release (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho et al. (2014) genetic rescue experiments.

claim: The inhibitory function of CPX requires a fully-folded and rigid CPX helix.
source: This is corroborated by functional data showing that the inhibitory function of CPX requires a fully-folded and rigid CPX helix (Radoff et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Radoff et al. (2014).

claim: Introducing flexibility within the minimal functional domain of CPX (residue 26-83) results in a reduction or loss of clamping ability corresponding to the degree of instability introduced.
source: and introducing flexibility within the minimal functional domain of CPX (residue 26–83) results in a reduction or loss of clamping ability corresponding to the degree of instability introduced (Kümmel et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014; Radoff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A single mutation in the CPXacc (F34M) results in two distinct binding interfaces for scCPX, both giving rise to the same zig-zag topology.
source: In fact, we found that a single mutation in the CPXacc (F34M) results in two distinct binding interfaces for scCPX, but both giving rise to the same zig-zag topology.
evidence: Based on structural analysis reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: Both F34M mutant binding interfaces involved the same face of CPXacc and t-SNARE, although the binding site on t-SNARE was extended by two helical turns for the mutant.
source: Both interactions involved the same face of CPXacc and t-SNARE, although the binding site on t-SNARE was extended by two helical turns for the mutant (Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on structural analysis reported in Kümmel et al. (2011).

claim: The trans clamping model remains the most well-defined model for which a good amount of evidence is available.
source: We do not consider the trans clamping model proven, but it remains the most well-defined model for which a good amount of evidence is available.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the state of evidence for their model.

claim: The trans CPXacc-t-SNARE interactions would lead to the formation of CPX/SNAREΔ60 polymers.
source: We note that the prediction from our model is that the trans CPXacc–t-SNARE interactions would lead to the formation of CPX/SNAREΔ60 polymers, which would not be visible in NMR studies due to line broadening.
evidence: Prediction from the trans clamping model.

claim: CPX/SNAREΔ60 polymers would not be visible in NMR studies due to line broadening.
source: We note that the prediction from our model is that the trans CPXacc–t-SNARE interactions would lead to the formation of CPX/SNAREΔ60 polymers, which would not be visible in NMR studies due to line broadening.
evidence: Based on known limitations of NMR for large complexes.

claim: The NMR technique may not be well suited for interrogation of trans interactions that lead to polymer formation.
source: Thus, if there is a trans interaction, then the NMR technique may not be well suited for its interrogation.
evidence: Inference based on the limitations of NMR for large oligomeric complexes.

claim: The cross-linked high-order oligomeric state of CPX-SNAREΔ60 is evident qualitatively in the ITC experiments where full-length CPX was titrated into unblocked SNAREΔ60.
source: This cross-linked high-order oligomeric state is evident qualitatively in the ITC experiments where we titrated full-length CPX into unblocked SNAREΔ60 (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on ITC experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The concentrations used in the NMR studies (~25-50 μM) correspond to the lower end of the range of concentration used for NMR studies.
source: We suspect that the concentrations used in the NMR studies (∼25–50 μM) (Trimbuch et al., 2014), which correspond to the lower end of the range of concentration used for NMR studies, were adjusted to avoid oligomerization and line broadening effects.
evidence: Authors' speculation about experimental design choices in Trimbuch et al.

claim: Under the NMR conditions of Trimbuch et al., most of the CPX-SNAREΔ60 complexes were likely monomeric, with only a small fraction in an oligomeric form.
source: it is plausible that, under the NMR conditions of Trimbuch et al., most of the CPX–SNAREΔ60 complexes were monomeric, with only a small fraction in an oligomeric form.
evidence: Authors' speculation based on concentration considerations and Kd values.

claim: The minor bound fraction of CPX-SNAREΔ60 oligomers would not be visible in NMR spectra owing to the large size of the cross-linked oligomers.
source: Thus, under the experimental conditions used by Trimbuch et al., CPXacc might not have an appreciable interaction with the t-SNARE groove, and the minor bound fraction would not be visible in NMR spectra owing to the large size of the cross-linked oligomers, assuming that there is no exchange between the monomeric and oligomeric forms of CPX–SNAREΔ60.
evidence: Authors' speculation about why NMR did not detect the interaction.

claim: The negative NMR data in Trimbuch et al. do not preclude a trans interaction between CPX and the SNAREΔ60 complex.
source: Therefore, we believe that the negative NMR data in Trimbuch et al. do not preclude a trans interaction between CPX and the SNAREΔ60 complex.
evidence: Authors' conclusion based on their analysis of the NMR limitations.

claim: Super clamp and non-clamp CPX mutations did not have the expected effect on evoked or spontaneous release in autaptic neuronal culture derived from CPX triple KO mice.
source: They found that the super clamp and non-clamp CPX mutations, which are predicted to enhance or decrease CPXacc–t-SNARE binding, respectively, did not have the expected effect on evoked or spontaneous release.
evidence: Reference to findings from Trimbuch et al. (2014).

claim: Both evoked and spontaneous release are reduced in CPX TKO mice.
source: Specifically, the inhibitory function of CPX has not been observed in the autaptic system: that is, both evoked and spontaneous release are reduced in CPX TKO mice (Reim et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2008; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in CPX TKO mice.

claim: In vivo studies support many of the observations made first with the cell-cell fusion assay.
source: In addition, these in vivo studies (Yang et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2014) support many of the observations made first with the cell–cell fusion assay (Giraudo et al., 2006, 2008, 2009; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011), underscoring the validity and the relevancy of the in vitro cell–cell fusion assay to study CPX clamping.
evidence: Comparison of in vivo and in vitro findings across multiple studies.

claim: Increasing the net negative charge on CPXacc inhibits neurotransmitter release.
source: This was based on the finding that increasing or decreasing the net negative charge on CPXacc inhibits or stimulates neurotransmitter release, respectively (Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: Reference to findings from Trimbuch et al. (2014).

claim: Decreasing the net negative charge on CPXacc stimulates neurotransmitter release.
source: This was based on the finding that increasing or decreasing the net negative charge on CPXacc inhibits or stimulates neurotransmitter release, respectively (Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: Reference to findings from Trimbuch et al. (2014).

claim: A number of both in vitro and in vivo studies on CPXacc modification argue strongly against the electrostatic hindrance model.
source: We note that a number of both in vitro and in vivo studies on CPXacc modification argue strongly against the electrostatic hindrance model (Yang et al., 2010; Kümmel et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014; Radoff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The conformations sampled by CPX26-48 are dependent on its protein context.
source: We suspect that the conformations sampled by CPX26–48 are dependent on its protein context, and this might account for the different binding affinities observed for the shorter (CPX26–48) compared with the longer (CPX26–83 and CPX1–134) constructs.
evidence: Authors' speculation based on observed differences in binding and structure.

claim: Yet unknown additional interactions in the pre-fusion complex may further stabilize the trans clamping interaction.
source: We also suspect that yet unknown additional interactions in the pre-fusion complex, which are not represented in our crystal structure, may further stabilize the trans clamping interaction (Cho et al., 2014; Radoff et al., 2014).
evidence: Authors' speculation about potential additional stabilizing interactions.

claim: Details of the interaction between wild-type CPXacc and t-SNARE must be different from those observed in the crystal structure with scCPX.
source: As we emphasized in Kümmel et al., we do not propose that the interactions are necessarily exactly as observed in a single crystal structure for which scCPX was used and where hydrophobic accessory helix residues (which are hydrophilic in wild-type CPX) interact with hydrophobic residues in a partially assembled SNARE complex. Details of the interaction between wild-type CPXacc and t-SNARE must be different (they are also weaker, explaining why the wild-type CPX clamps less well)
evidence: Authors' inference based on differences between scCPX and wild-type CPX.

claim: Wild-type CPXacc interactions with t-SNARE are weaker than scCPX interactions, explaining why wild-type CPX clamps less well.
